Why it exists

AI can build our screens in minutes. It builds everyone's screens.

Speed is solved. The new risk is sameness — an AI with no source of truth reaches for generic defaults, and our products stop looking like ours. The fix is to write the brain down once, in a form machines are obliged to read.

The experiment

We asked an AI for a contract-analysis screen.

The result wasn't Orbit — it was a generic multi-step wizard, because the real knowledge lived scattered across the codebase, people's heads, screenshots, and policy docs.

The answer

Put the knowledge where the machine looks.

One governed vault of contracts, tokens, and rules that every tool reads before it builds — so the output is Orbit by construction, not by luck.

What it is

A shared brain, not a slide deck.

The vault holds the actual specifications our products are built to — written once, referenced everywhere, and kept honest by automated checks. It replaces scattered, conflicting guidance with one authoritative place.

01

Single source of truth

Designers, engineers, and AI tools all read the same contracts. No more "which version of the button is right?"

02

Two platforms, one foundation

Connected Platform (internal Efficio users) and Orbit / Client Connected Platform (external clients) share a base, and diverge only where they should.

03

Built for AI-assisted delivery

Machine-readable rules route each task to the right specialist agent — so AI builds to our standards instead of generic defaults.

04

Governed & self-checking

Changes go through review; CI catches broken links, missing metadata, and stale docs before they spread.

How the tools connect

The vault is the hub. Every tool orbits it.

Real code flows in to keep the brain honest; the brain flows out to the tools that build; and corrections flow back. Obsidian and Git aren't separate consumers — they're how the vault itself is authored and distributed.

How it's governed

Author here first. Export everywhere second.

Nothing changes the products directly. Every change is authored in the vault, approved by design-system owners, checked by CI, and only then exported into the product repositories.

The orchestration layer

11 specialist agents — each on the right-sized model.

Rather than one AI doing everything, work is split across specialists. The rule is simple: the more a task is pinned down in writing, the cheaper the model it needs; the more it depends on judgment, the stronger the model we put on it.

context-scoutHaiku

Assembles the context packet — which files, which platform, which agent a task needs.

vault-librarianin-reviewHaiku

Link checks, metadata lint, staleness sweeps; triages the corrections inbox.

component-builderSonnet

Builds or refactors one component to its written contract.

contract-extractorSonnet

Reads real source code and writes the component contract for it.

porterin-reviewSonnet

Ports external / Lovable prototypes onto Orbit tokens and components.

screen-builderin-reviewSonnet

Composes multi-component screens from the page patterns.

story-authordraftSonnet

Builder agent

benchmark-judgein-reviewOpus

Blind A/B scoring for quality benchmarks — the scoring-integrity gate.

brief-coachdraftOpus

Draws a testable concept brief out of a stakeholder through questions — never judges it.

brief-reviewerin-reviewOpus

Independently gates a concept brief against the contract, blind to the coaching.

design-reviewerOpus

Judges finished work against the brain — fresh eyes, never grading its own build.

HaikuSonnetOpus
More written constraint → cheaper model. More judgment → stronger model. The strongest model reviews the work — because rework costs more than review, and the builder never certifies its own output.

Who writes it, who reads it

Authors write the vault. Consumers never touch it.

A clean split keeps the source of truth trustworthy: a small set of authors edit the vault; everyone else — including the AI tools — reads a generated, read-only export.

Does it work?

We benchmark the brain the way engineers benchmark code.

Every claim here is measured against tasks in _benchmarks/ — not asserted.

17/18

Compliance, on task

A form-with-validation build scored 17 of 18 on the compliance rubric (tokens, components, states, a11y) — a pass.

15 vs 7

The right design wins

On the flow rubric (/16) the well-structured build scored 15; a compliance-perfect wizard scored 7 — more than double.

18/18

Yet still UX-poor

An output can ace compliance and still be hard to use — which is exactly why a separate craft rubric (/10) now runs alongside it.

One investment, four returns

Every team plugs into the same brain.
